strong_form: Innovators whose key capability was self-taught produce markedly fewer eminent students than innovators trained in master-apprentice lineages, and no known method reliably passes self-teaching on.
weak_form: Self-teaching is hard to transmit, and eminence often runs through apprenticeship chains rather than through lone autodidacts.
refuted_if: A bibliometric comparison shows self-taught or outsider innovators have as many eminent students as lineage-trained ones, or an intervention measurably raises autodidactic ability in students.

prior_art.citation: Physics-L archive: Einstein 'had no school (like Bohr)'; later envied Bohr for founding a school
Physics-L reply noting Pais describes some Einstein students
Zuckerman, Scientific Elite: 48 of 92 US laureates trained under laureates; Nobel subnetworks span four generations
Oxford study of the UK scientific ultra-elite replicating Zuckerman's selection processes

strongest_criticism: Einstein having no school may reflect his career (few teaching posts, solitary style, opposition to quantum mechanics) rather than self-teaching. Einstein was also not really self-taught: he trained at ETH. The Zuckerman lineage data show that schools transmit eminence, but nobody has done the matched comparison of self-taught versus trained masters. 'Nobody knows how' cannot be refuted by any single observation.
